extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general mathematically-interested readers (readers with a modest undergraduate mathematics background); mathematicians and students seeking elegant, elementary proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and informal standards for selecting and presenting "Book Proofs": short, elegant, elementary, insightful mathematical proofs that are accessible to readers with modest undergraduate preparation. Emphasis on multiple viewpoints, clear notation, and pedagogical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: No strict definition of a "Book Proof"
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have no definition or characterization of what constitutes a proof from The Book: all we offer here is the examples that we have selected, hoping that our readers will share our enthusiasm about brilliant ideas, clever insights and wonderful observations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the notion of a "Book Proof" as aesthetic and example-driven rather than formally defined; selection is guided by mathematical beauty, insight, and the authors' taste (strongly influenced by Paul Erdős).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / assumed background
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything in this book is supposed to be accessible to readers whose backgrounds include only a modest amount of technique from undergraduate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required background: a little linear algebra, some basic analysis and number theory, and elementary discrete mathematics. Choose presentations and proofs that can be followed with this level of preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and aesthetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the dictum (G. H. Hardy) that 'there is no permanent place for ugly mathematics' — proofs should be brief, elegant and aesthetically pleasing where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, illuminating arguments; avoid proofs that require long, messy technical details. The authors omitted a chapter ('problem of the thirteen spheres') because its proof could not be made 'brief and elegant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary-method preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor proofs that use elementary or classical techniques rather than heavy machinery when a clear, insightful elementary proof exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present elementary or combinatorial proofs when possible (e.g., Euclid-style arguments, combinatorial or number-theoretic proofs, Erdős' elementary approaches). Note also historical remarks about elementary vs. complex-analytic proofs (e.g., elementary proofs of the prime number theorem by Selberg and Erdős).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple viewpoints and plurality of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Display several different proofs of the same statement to illuminate different viewpoints and ideas (e.g., 'Six proofs of the infinity of primes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructive, include multiple proofs that use distinct ideas (algebraic, analytic, topological, combinatorial, probabilistic) to highlight the core reason a result is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight key lemmas / the 'crux' of the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and label the pivotal steps or lemmas in an argument (the authors explicitly mark 'the crux' or 'key fact' in proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the central idea of each proof visible (boxes, lemmas, or textual emphasis) so readers can grasp the main insight before getting lost in details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix notation and present supporting boxed results
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix notation early (e.g., N, Z, P) and present frequently used fundamental results in boxed or isolated form (examples: Lagrange's Theorem, Legendre's Theorem, 'Prime fields' box).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clear definitions and isolate standard lemmas/theorems with short proofs or citations so that proofs remain readable and self-contained at the intended level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative figures and diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures and illustrations liberally to aid understanding (the book advertises 'With 250 Figures' and credits an illustrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany geometric, combinatorial, or conceptual arguments with diagrams to make key configurations and ideas immediately clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical context and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide historical remarks, original attributions, and motivations (many topics and proofs are presented with credit to Erdős, Euclid, Euler, Fürstenberg, Ramanujan, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate proofs within their historical development, note originators and variants of proofs, and mention reasons authors chose particular presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical organization and gradual progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material by topic and complexity (table of contents groups number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, graph theory) and present warm-ups, lemmas, and stronger theorems in a pedagogical sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with classical or motivating examples, provide warm-up proofs or lemmas, then progress to more sophisticated results; include appendices for auxiliary estimation techniques and methods.
